bandReport.notes: *** PAGE-MAP DEFECT — READ THIS FIRST. My assigned band was pages 4,6,8,10 on the stated assumption that this booklet opens with THREE cover pages so the English run starts at index 4. IT DOES NOT. Page index 2 is an ENGLISH content page (footer '( 3 - A )') carrying the 'Directions for the following 8 (eight) items' block, Passage-1, Passage-2 and ITEMS 1, 2 and 3. Page index 4 opens at Passage-3 / item 4. I verified the alternation rather than assuming it: page index 3 is the HINDI mirror of page 4 (same Passage-3/Passage-4, same items 4 and 5), so English genuinely is the EVEN 0-based index and the first English content page is 2, not 4. config.ts has `evens(4, 42)` for 2019-p2; the correct list is `evens(2, 42)` (21 English pages, not 20). Page 2 is not in ANY band's assignment, so items 1-3 would have been silently missing from the whole paper. Because b1 is designated the first band and must start at item 1, I rendered page 2 myself from the source PDF (C:/Vilas/LWS_Pune/UPSC/Paper-2/csp-p2.pdf, index 2) at 200/220 dpi with overlapping column crops, transcribed it, and included items 1-3 here. Page 2 is therefore listed in `pages` and `itemsByPage` above even though it was not assigned. ACTION OWED BY A MAINTAINER: fix config.ts to evens(2,42) and re-render, so the crops are reproducible from the pipeline rather than from my scratchpad. RELATED, NOT VERIFIED BY ME: if the English run is shifted by one page at the start, the TAIL may be shifted too — the config stops at 42 in a 48-page booklet. Someone owning the tail pages should confirm that item 80 really is reached by page 42 and that pages 44/46 are not English content. I did not open them; they are outside my three bands. --- COLUMN-CROP CHECK ON THE GUTTER-FALLBACK PAGES. Two of my b1 pages are on the fallback list (4 and 10; gutterFound=false in _render.json). I opened pNN.png for both and compared against the c1/c2 crops: BOTH ARE USABLE. On page 4 the split landed just to the RIGHT of the printed vertical rule, so c1 holds the whole left column intact (Passage-3 + all of item 4 incl. all four options) and carries only a narrow sliver of column 2's left edge; c2 holds the whole right column intact (Passage-4 + all of item 5). Page 10 is the same shape: c1 holds items 12, 13, 14 whole and c2 holds items 15, 16, 17 whole, with only marginal fragments bleeding across. No line was cut down its middle on either page and no item number was lost from the top of c2. Page 2, which I cropped myself, was cut with a deliberate +/-1.5% overlap for the same reason, so nothing could fall in the gap. --- SEAM I DO NOT OWN THE FAR SIDE OF: none at the start (page 2 is the first content page of the paper). The 10/12 seam is internal to my own work (b1 ends page 10, b2 starts page 12): item 17 completes in full on page 10 and page 12 opens cleanly at item 18, so nothing straddles it. --- PRINTED / SCAN DEFECTS. (i) Page 2, Passage-1, near the end: the word 'discrimination' in 'but because one or the other wrong, generally discrimination, tends to acquire partial autonomy' has an ink blot covering the initial 'd', so it images as a filled blob followed by 'iscrimination'. This is scan/print damage over a letter, not a printed variant reading, and the word is unambiguous from context and from the identical word twice earlier in the same passage; transcribed as 'discrimination'. (ii) Page 2, Passage-1, line 4: 'a variety of historical wrongs that continue' carries a stray ink mark on the 'a' of 'that', imaging as 'thdt'. Same class; transcribed as 'that'. (iii) RAISED MIDDLE DOT decimals preserved as U+00B7 exactly as printed, NOT as a full stop: Q11 options (b) '45·5%' and (d) '37·5%', and Q16 option (d) '16·5'. (iv) Q12 prints its ordinals as superscripts (5th Monday, 5th Thursday, 20th December); transcribed as plain 'th' since the superscript is typographic, not mathematical. (v) Q17 uses the rupee sign, preserved as ₹. No duplicate option text and no missing/blank option anywhere in items 1-17. --- CONTEXT MAPPING. The 'Directions for the following 8 (eight) items' block on page 2 governs items 1-8 across SEVEN passages, and the mapping is NOT one passage per item: Passage-1 governs items 1 AND 2 (two items, identical context string byte-for-byte on both), while Passages 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 govern exactly one item each (items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 respectively). Six single-item contexts will therefore raise 'lonely-context' warnings at merge; they are correct, not defects — the passage is genuinely shared material printed above its item, and the existing 2020-p2 bands carry four of the same shape. The directions preamble itself is deliberately NOT in any context field. Items 9-17 are standalone numeracy/reasoning with no passage and no context. --- ITEM 13 prints its statements as arabic '1. 2. 3.' and its conclusions as roman 'I. II. III.'; both lists kept on their own lines in the stem exactly as printed.

questions.context: Political theorists no doubt have to take history of injustice, for example, untouchability, seriously. The concept of historical injustice takes note of a variety of historical wrongs that continue into the present in some form or the other and tend to resist repair. Two reasons might account for resistance to repair. One, not only are the roots of injustice buried deep in history, injustice itself constitutes economic structures of exploitation, ideologies of discrimination and modes of representation. Two, the category of historical injustice generally extends across a number of wrongs such as economic deprivation, social discrimination and lack of recognition. This category is complex, not only because of the overlap between a number of wrongs, but because one or the other wrong, generally discrimination, tends to acquire partial autonomy from others. This is borne out by the history of repair in India.
questions.stem: What is the main idea that we can infer from the passage ?

options.label: A
options.text: Untouchability in India has not been taken seriously by political theorists.

options.label: B
options.text: Historical injustice is inevitable in any society and is always beyond repair.

options.label: C
options.text: Social discrimination and deprivation have their roots in bad economies.

options.label: D
options.text: It is difficult, if not impossible, to repair every manifestation of historical injustice.

questions.context: Education plays a great transformatory role in life, particularly so in this rapidly changing and globalizing world. Universities are the custodians of the intellectual capital and promoters of culture and specialized knowledge. Culture is an activity of thought, and receptiveness to beauty and human feelings. A merely well informed man is only a bore on God's earth. What we should aim at is producing men who possess both culture and expert knowledge. Their expert knowledge will give them a firm ground to start from and their culture will lead them as deep as philosophy and as high as art. Together it will impart meaning to human existence.

Soil can trap huge quantities of carbon dioxide in the form of organic carbon and prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.

questions.context: Inequality is visible, even statistically measurable in many instances, but the economic power that drives it is invisible and not measurable. Like the force of gravity, power is the organising principle of inequality, be it of income, or wealth, gender, race, religion and region. Its effects are seen in a pervasive manner in all spheres, but the ways in which economic power pulls and tilts visible economic variables remain invisibly obscure.

questions.context: Climate change may actually benefit some plants by lengthening growing seasons and increasing carbon dioxide. Yet other effects of a warmer world, such as more pests, droughts, and flooding, will be less benign. How will the world adapt ? Researchers project that by 2050, suitable croplands for four commodities — maize, potatoes, rice and wheat — will shift, in some cases pushing farmers to plant new crops. Some farmlands may benefit from warming, but others won't. Climate alone does not dictate yields; political shifts, global demand, and agricultural practices will influence how farms fare in the future.

questions.context: A bat's wings may look like sheets of skin. But underneath, a bat has the same five fingers as an orangutan or a human, as well as a wrist connected to the same cluster of wrist bones connected to the same long bones of the arm. What can be more curious than that the hand of a man, formed for grasping, that of a mole for digging, the leg of the horse, the paddle of the porpoise, and the wing of the bat, should all be constructed on the same pattern ?

questions.context: Around 56 million years ago, the Atlantic Ocean had not fully opened and animals, perhaps including our primate ancestors, could walk from Asia to North America through Europe and across Greenland. Earth was warmer than it is today, but as the Palaeocene epoch gave way to Eocene, it was about to get much warmer still — rapidly and radically. The cause was a massive geologically sudden release of carbon. During this period called Palaeocene – Eocene Thermal Maximum or PETM, the carbon injected into the atmosphere was roughly the amount that would be injected today if humans burned all the Earth's reserves of coal, oil and natural gas. The PETM lasted for about 1,50,000 years, until the excess carbon was reabsorbed. It brought on drought, floods, insect plagues and a few extinctions. Life on Earth survived — indeed, it prospered — but it was drastically different.

3. Increased warming of Earth's atmosphere can change the composition of its flora and fauna.
4. The present man-made global warming will finally lead to conditions similar to those which happened 56 million years ago.
Which of the assumptions given above are valid ?
